tagline.text: A folk museum in Bontoc gathering the cultures of the Cordillera peoples

location.label: Location
location.text: Poblacion, Bontoc, Mountain Province, inside a Catholic convent compound

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,000 (Bontoc day visit, transport not included)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), then overland

children.text: Bontoc Museum is a folk museum in Bontoc, the capital of Mountain Province, where you can see everyday tools, old photographs and a replica of a traditional village from the Cordillera highland peoples, including the Ifugao, Bontoc and Kalinga, all in one place. It makes a good half-day stop between Sagada and Banaue.

Bontoc Museum is a small folk museum in the town of Bontoc, the capital of Mountain Province in the Cordillera region of northern Philippines. It is often called the Bontoc Village Museum, and it collects the daily life, tools, beliefs and former ways of the highland peoples of the area, commonly grouped under the name Igorot. The building is modeled on a traditional Bontoc house with a pointed roof, and its three linked roofs make it easy to spot from a distance.

The museum is said to have grown out of the work of Belgian Catholic missionary sisters (ICM) who settled in Bontoc. One travel blog names the founder as Mother Basil Gekiere, who lived in Bontoc for 56 years and died in 1983. It is now cared for by the Diocese of Bontoc, and it stands inside the compound of the convent and St. Vincent's Elementary School. Sources disagree on the founding year, so it is not given here.

The exhibits fall into two parts: indoor galleries, and an outdoor replica of a traditional village behind the building. Indoors, artifacts from the Ifugao, Bontoc and Kalinga areas are divided by room. Outdoors, the layout of an old village is recreated, including the ato and ulog, the communal buildings used by young men and young women, as well as a pig pen. The museum is not large, and one to two hours is enough even at a slow pace.

Rather than expecting spectacle, think of it as a place that gives you the background for what you meet while traveling the Cordillera, such as the burial caves of Sagada, the rice terraces of Banaue and the tattooing of Buscalan, and the lives those sights came from. Bontoc lies between Sagada and Banaue and on the way north to Kalinga, so it is easy to stop here along the route. The town sits at an average elevation of about 1,173 m, has a population of about 23,000 as of 2024, and is roughly 387 km from Manila. It was once the central town of the Cordillera.

The indoor galleries show artifacts of the Ifugao, Bontoc and Kalinga, divided by room. You will see everyday tools, musical instruments and small models of traditional houses, and one blog says most Igorot instruments and tools are on display. It lets you compare how tools and customs differ from one part of the Cordillera to another.

Behind the building is an outdoor exhibit that recreates an old Bontoc village. You can walk through a furnished model of a Bontoc house, a smithy, fish traps, a low-ceilinged hut and a vegetable garden. Many visitors say this part stays in the memory, and in photographs, longer than the indoor rooms.

The ato is described as a sacred place where village elders and leaders gathered to settle community matters and hold rituals and dances, and where boys at puberty also stayed to learn their culture. The ulog was a communal dormitory where young women lived together and learned the traditions of their tribe. The custom is fading today, so seeing the structure, even as a replica, is meaningful.

The galleries hang old photographs of everyday life among the Cordillera peoples, and they are known to include pictures from the headhunting era. Captions mix English with local terms and take time to read, but they give a sense of a highland village a century ago.

Rock and fossil specimens from the Cordillera mountains are also on display. This corner of natural geology among the cultural exhibits is a reminder that the region is a highland area well over 1,000 m above sea level.

Wikipedia notes that Bontoc town has two National Cultural Treasures, the Stone Agricultural Calendar of Bontoc and the Alab Petroglyphs. After the broad picture of tribal culture at the museum, seeing these as well gives you a fuller understanding of the old farming and beliefs of the Cordillera. The Alab Petroglyphs were submitted to UNESCO's Tentative List in 2006.

blocks.title: Remembering the Chico River dam fight

children.text: In the 1970s, Bontoc and nearby towns faced flooding under the Marcos government's Chico River dam plan, and the Bontoc and Kalinga peoples joined forces through a peace pact (bodong) to oppose it. The resistance led to the project being abandoned, and April 24 is observed as Cordillera Day. Seeing the role of tribal elders in the museum helps you understand this history better.

A library, the Museum Ethno-Cordillera Library, and a gift shop stand in a building separate from the main museum. The library has a limited collection but offers local folk-culture material, and the gift shop is said to sell postcards and small wood carvings. Their opening hours may differ from the museum's, so check on site.

items.title: A half day passing through Bontoc
items.subtitle: The museum and a walk around town

children.text: Eat breakfast near your lodging or the terminal in Bontoc, then walk toward the museum. Visitors report about
15 minutes
on foot from the town center, and a tricycle is also close.
Enter when it opens. The entrance fee is reported at between
, so bring small change. Go through the indoor galleries slowly, in the order Ifugao, Bontoc, Kalinga. Most visitors report that photography is not allowed indoors.
Walk around the outdoor replica village behind the building. As you look at the ato, ulog, smithy and pig pen, match the terms you saw in the galleries to the actual structures.
Pick out a postcard or a small souvenir at the library and gift shop, then return to town.
Have lunch at a restaurant near Bontoc market. Some visitors report that the museum closes at lunchtime, so if you plan to return in the afternoon, check the hours.
Because the museum is small, many travelers finish in the morning and head to Sagada or the Maligcong rice terraces in the afternoon. Check bus times again locally.

Buses are reported from the Governor Pack Road area in Baguio at 8:00 AM, 10:00 AM and 2:30 PM. The fare is about
Another company leaves from the Slaughter House Compound whenever full, from 5:00 AM to 1:00 PM. Both schedules change often.
Bontoc is a small town and you can walk to most places. Visitors report about

When it is hot or you have luggage, take a tricycle, and agree the fare beforehand.

The museum is mostly indoors, so you can visit in any weather, but the outdoor village replica and getting around town are much easier in the dry season. Bontoc is a mountain town at about 1,173 m, so days are cool and mornings and nights are chilly.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
Bontoc is the capital of Mountain Province but is a small, quiet town. Guesthouses and small lodgings are in the town center, and a night is known to cost about
. Many guides say you do not need to book ahead except during the first week of April, when the Lang-ay Festival is held, but it is safest to check recent rates and vacancies before you arrive.
For meals, go to local restaurants and small eateries around the town market. Because this is mountain country, vegetable, rice and pork dishes are common, and a meal costs about

. The postcards and small wood carvings sold at the museum gift shop are easy to carry home. The town is small enough to walk, so after the museum, a slow walk through the market, the church and the shopping streets fills a half day well. If you arrive late and the museum has closed, plan to drop in early the next morning.
Entrance fees and opening hours differ from one report to another. Some say weekdays 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM and Sundays afternoon only, so avoid Sundays or check first.
Some visitors report that it closes for lunch (12:00 to 1:00 PM), so it is safest to arrive around 9:00 AM or after 1:00 PM.
Many visitors report that photos and video are not allowed in the indoor galleries. Ask for guidance about the outdoor area.
Bring small cash (₱20 and ₱50 notes). Change may be short.
Exhibit labels contain many local terms, so asking staff or a sister for an explanation will teach you more.
The museum is close enough to walk from the Bontoc terminal, but take a tricycle on rainy days.
Sagada and Banaue are long mountain trips, so we recommend spending a night in Bontoc.
The museum stands in a compound run by a religious organization, so dress and behave modestly, and do not touch or climb on the replica village.
Check the latest notices for fees and hours. Some reports are old and may differ from today.
In the rainy season, mountain roads to Bontoc (such as the Halsema Highway) often have landslides and fog, so avoid night travel.
Some customs shown (headhunting, communal dormitories) differ from today's standards, so view the exhibits with respect, as the history of a people.
ATMs are scarce in this region, so bring cash from Bontoc or Baguio. One guide notes that mountain towns such as Barlig have no ATM.
The museum may close temporarily for repairs or events.
